#382. Inspired by Bernie Sanders: A German agency is using US-Style campaigning to boost the left in 2029

"The Goodforces" wants to see a swing to the left in the 2029 German elections. The agency counts New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Bernie Sanders among its inspirations. Could it transform the political landscape?

Red, red, green — those are the party colors of the left-leaning coalition recently formed in the German state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. Now a Berlin-based agency wants to see the same alliance between the center-left Social Democrats, the socialist Left Party, and environmentalist Greens win the 2029 national elections.

The Goodforces wants to help make that a reality with their campaign neunund20 (twenty-nine), taking its cue, in part, from the American left. The agency was set up in response to the rise of the far right across Europe.

Co-founder Patrick Haermeyer told DW that the campaign's aim is "to give people hope and an alternative narrative to: Things are getting worse and worse." He worked as an online organizer for the election team of Bernie Sanders in the US Democratic presidential primaries in 2016 and cites Sanders' "not me, us" campaign as an inspiration.

Neunund20 currently has two strategies: It provides digital space for short-form videos and social media content on political and social topics on Instagram, Tiktok, and Bluesky. At the same time, it tries to connect content creators, activists, NGOs, and political initiatives around shared "progressive" issues.

Users with a particular interest can click to get a link giving them access to archives of relevant social media material that they can then reshare. That feature is modelled on the campaign of New York's left-wing mayor Zohran Mamdani.

And there are other projects. The Goodforces was recently involved in a tactical voting initiative in the September elections in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, intended to keep the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) from winning an absolute majority. Haermeyer says physical campaigns of that kind are necessary to provide essential "interim victories" en route to the next parliamentary elections.

The Greens and the SPD, the two parties recommended by the app created by the organization, made it over the 5% hurdle and into parliament. The help that they received was declared by each party in the form of a €40,000 ($43,900) donation.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The agency sees itself as a kind of Super PAC, modeled on political organizations in the United States that collect money to carry out campaigns without directly supporting a single party or a special candidate.

For Christoph Bieber, political scientist at the University of Duisburg-Essen, the Goodforces is an interesting new type of player on Germany's political scene because it operates outside the country's political parties.

But many of those parties are eyeing the development with disquiet. The far-left, populist, immigration skeptical Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW) criticized the Goodforces' intervention in Saxony-Anhalt, telling the newspaper FAZ that it was an "infantilizing, and perhaps even antidemocratic action." The neoliberal Free Democrats (FDP) called the tool "wrong and intentionally misleading." The FDP failed to clear the threshold, while the BSW only just squeaked in. The AfD gained 43% of the vote and its candidate may soon become Germany's first far-right state premier since the Nazi era.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Haermeyer set up the agency in 2024 along with Peter Jelinek, and both men previously worked for Green Party European Parliament member Michael Bloss. Ahead of that year's European elections, the EU's Green Deal began to come under increasing attack.

That year also ended with the collapse of Germany's first federal coalition between the SPD, Greens, and FDP, after much infighting and attacks from right-wing quarters.

"We noticed that more and more successes and freedoms that we had fought for were being reversed: Things like freedom of movement, border checks, and other things that were coming more and more under fire," Haermeyer told DW. "And we noticed that it was primarily democratic and progressive forces that were being drawn into defensive battles."

The AfD, founded in 2013, already in the age of social media, has successfully targeted younger voters with in its online campaigns. But the older parties, in particular, have struggled. The Goodforces saw a need for support in the online environment and is now seeking to plug this gap.

The social media accounts of the campaign neunund20 contain posts on domestic German topics, such as the current negotiations to form a red-red-green coalition government in Berlin, and the country's new military service law. They also highlight "wins" in Spain in the protests for affordable housing and for US Democrats in the midterms.

Haermeyer stresses that the issues the agency highlights are determined together with a wide range of grassroots organizations and activists. "The campaign is not agreed in conjunction with the SPD, the Left Party, and the Greens," he said.

Agency funding comes from commissions and small donations. Haermeyer says that contributions generally range from $20 to $50.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Bieber sees the emergence of non-party campaigning, long an accepted practice in the US, as a bid to compensate for the shortcomings of traditional parties.

"It is an omission of the parties," he said. "For years they have been saying we have to modernize, we have to become more open and get away from rigid membership structures. There are legal regulations governing the organization of political parties in Germany, but perhaps it could be more flexible and open."

The center-left and center-right big-tent parties have been in decline for decades. Membership of the SPD dropped from 943,000 in 1990 to some 348,000 at the end of 2025. Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) has seen a fall from 750,000 to under 357,000.

Party membership is particularly low in former communist eastern Germany. Centrist parties have also struggled to attract younger voters. A report by the Deutsche Kinder und Jugendstiftung (German Children and Youth Foundation) showed that only 20% of young people felt their concerns were taken seriously in the 2025 German elections and that trust in parties was low.

In the United States, campaign financing comes predominantly from donations, and lobby groups can buy influence by contributing unlimited amounts to super PACs. In Germany, party funding comes, in part, from taxpayers and membership fees, and donations are capped. However, Bieber warns that whereas there are strict rules regarding the disclosure of donors to US Super PACs, these do not exist in Germany.

The political scientist does not believe that US-style campaigning is going to take hold in Germany, but he does see potential dangers: "This could be a door opener to make others consider whether they want to go in this direction in the field of campaigning. And he added: "If it becomes rife, it could lead to a further devaluation of parties and their structures."

#380. International first class is over for U.S. airlines. Enter the mega business-class cabin

The era of U.S. airlines' long-haul, international first class ended this week when American Airlines' last flight with its eight-suite section landed. In its place will be a massive business-class cabin with room for 70 passengers.

U.S. airlines have been ditching international first-class cabins for a new top tier: larger and souped-up business classes, featuring suites with sliding doors, the design du jour. Delta Air Lines and United Airlines have already taken this step. American was the last of the U.S. airlines to still have first class on long-haul international routes.

Many travelers might not notice the difference. That's because of airlines' investments into business class: new suites, bigger screens, better technology like device-charging pads, and improved bedding.

It's part of airlines' big bet on mass luxury. Consumers have been willing to shell out more to fly comfortably, which is helping to boost airline revenue. That's all the more important as costs of everything from fuel to airport landing fees have been rising, soaking up more of the industry's profits.

The retirement of first class ends a more-than-six-decade stretch of the jet age that in the early days included service like seat-side carving of chateaubriand and meals served on fine bone china.

A few decades ago, business class was much smaller, with two-by-two seats in some configurations, and recliners, not the lie-flat seats that dominate those cabins now.

"When you've got individual pods in biz class, and you've got a comfortable enough seat and bedding and decent wine, for a lot of people this is good enough," said Henry Harteveldt, founder of travel consulting firm Atmosphere Research Group and a former airline executive.

The over-the-top dining of the early days of international first class was a form of entertainment, long before laptops, personal seat-back screens and in-flight Wi-Fi, or even the promise of sleep on lie-flat beds, but customers still eat lots on board, Harteveldt said.

"People say they want to sleep but then they stay up and they eat every morsel," he said. "They're hypocrites."

There was still a hefty price gap between first and business.

A flight between Los Angeles and London on American's Boeing 777-300ER this week went for $12,994 in business class for a one-way ticket and $15,669 for a first-class seat.

American's last flight with international first class departed Friday morning local time in Sydney, bound for Los Angeles.

Its new cabin on its Boeing 777-300ERs will feature 70 business-class suites, the most of any U.S. airline. Pre-overhaul, the cabins had been operating with eight first-class suites and 52 pods in business, though the remodeling is ongoing. American is also flying a subfleet of 787-9 Dreamliners that have 51 business-class suites. (United is putting 64 new suites on that aircraft.)

Part of the allure is that some companies allow employees to book business-class tickets, but not first class.

American Airlines told CNBC it's growing its business-class cabins across the fleet. It's evaluating increasing the number of suites on its smaller long-haul jets, the Boeing 787-8 Dreamliners, from 20 currently to somewhere in the 30s.

"You don't have enough seats to make the seat cost competitive," Nat Pieper, American's chief commercial officer, said in an interview this month. "So what you need to do to make that airplane work is it's got to be a yield play. You need more business-class seats."

Differences between first and business classes on American lately came down to details.

On American's first-class long-haul section, passengers got olives with warm nuts to accompany their beverage early in the flight, while there were no olives for business class.

First class got a soup; business did not. First class got a warm dessert served a la mode in addition to the cold dessert or fruit and cheese plate both cabins were offered.

And there was no memory foam lumbar pillow for business class like there was in first, American said. But otherwise, the experiences were fairly similar for passengers. They still got better food options and service than economy passengers, along with their bigger seats, early boarding and lounge access.

"It's not like the bed can go any flatter than 180 degrees," Harteveldt said. "The bedding can be thicker, and the food nicer."

Delta and United have already replaced international, long-haul first class with dozens of their Delta One and Polaris business lie-flat suites, respectively, each of which is getting upgrades now.

American will continue offering a separate lie-flat first class on its Airbus A321T subfleet it uses for domestic cross-country flying until early 2027. But then that goes away, too.

Meanwhile, airlines over the past decade have added a premium economy section, which sits between business class and economy. It features recliner seats similar to those in domestic first class, often with foot rests, meals served on actual plates, larger seat-back screens than economy and earlier boarding.

Airlines are now cutting up business class into different segments, something they've done for more than a decade with the coach cabin's basic economy, standard and extra legroom seats.

United and Delta this year each announced their most expensive cabins will be sold with basic options, which are more restrictive and don't include things like the ability to pick your seat ahead of time or get access to a special airport lounge.

There are also a few seats in some of the business-class cabins that are roomier, like American's Flagship Suite Preferred and United's Polaris Studio. Even the guest seating in the United suite varies with "standard and companion ottomans," the latter including a seatbelt so you can ask "another Polaris passenger to visit you between takeoff and landing for a drink, chat or game," the airline says.

"I don't think we found the limit on segmentation," United CFO Mike Leskinen told CNBC on Thursday. "We have a few things on the drawing board. We're not done."

Although U.S. carriers are moving away from the designation, first class is far from dead.

Singapore Airlines, Germany's Lufthansa, British Airways and Air France have unveiled updated first-class cabins and other service improvements like food.

British Airways last month said it will build a record 106-suite business class on its Airbus A380 aircraft, the world's largest passenger airplane, but it's also upgrading its first class on board.

Meanwhile, smaller airlines like JetBlue Airways, Frontier Airlines and Allegiant Air are introducing domestic or short-haul first-class seats.

"We're going to be able to do that at a really low price comparatively to what you're used to out there in the marketplace," Frontier Chief Commercial Officer Bobby Schroeter said last month.

#375. Employees at Eric Trump-backed robot startup lose health benefits as company's cash crunch deepens

Employees at Foundation Future Industries were told that their health benefits through administrator Rippling have been terminated, according to a memo obtained by CNBC, adding to mounting signs of financial distress at the humanoid robot startup advised and backed by Eric Trump.

Foundation told staff in a Friday evening email that they'd be offered coverage through COBRA, the federal law that generally lets workers temporarily keep their health insurance after losing benefits by paying the full premium out of pocket.

"Because our last pay run through Rippling was in October, they have ended our benefits with them retroactive to October," a Foundation human resources manager said in the memo. "COBRA will be offered to all employees to cover November."

Foundation has garnered headlines for the bold claims that co-founder Sankaet Pathak — whose previous startup collapsed in 2024 — has made about his robots and their potential use in war zones. Employees were last paid on Oct. 15, and some inside the company are angry at Pathak for a $4.6 million loan he took from his company last year, CNBC reported earlier this month.

A Foundation spokesman didn't immediately respond to an email or phone call seeking comment.

In the staff memo, Foundation blamed Rippling for the disruption to health coverage. The startup also said it would reimburse COBRA premiums paid by workers and that it was onboarding a new benefits provider.

But employees, especially those whose family members are undergoing treatment for medical ailments, worry the company won't have funds to reimburse workers or reinstate coverage, people with direct knowledge of the situation said.

In a statement to CNBC, Rippling indicated it was Foundation's failure to pay for its employee benefits that led to the change: "If a client enrolled in Rippling's [Professional Employer Organization] is unable to meet their payroll and benefits obligations for multiple months, they will first receive a warning and if not met, they are terminated."

Foundation has been seeking a bridge loan to repay employees after its financial woes began in August. It has been in talks with three or four venture capital firms, including existing investor Tribe Capital, Pathak has told employees, according to people familiar with the situation, who asked to remain unnamed because they were not authorized to speak publicly and feared retaliation. Tribe didn't immediately return a request for comment.

The bridge loan would help the company survive until a possible $150 million investment from South Korean conglomerate Base Group lands as early as December or January, Pathak has told employees, the people said.

Base confirmed to Reuters in recent days that it was considering an investment, but the funding has not been finalized.

The potential investment would deepen business ties between the Trump family and the South Korean conglomerate, an aluminum producer also known for real estate and hospitality projects.

Base paid the Trump Organization $2 million in 2025, according to a New York Times article, drawing scrutiny from Democratic senators over conflict-of-interest concerns. Base has also pursued other business relationships with the Trump Organization, including a Trump-branded golf course in South Korea.

Eric Trump, who has invested in Foundation and was given the title of chief strategy advisor, didn't immediately respond to a CNBC email seeking comment.

The prospect of employees having to pay for their own health coverage comes as many are already drawing down savings to cover living expenses. With another scheduled payday approaching on Nov. 30, workers are facing a third straight pay cycle without income.

Many are actively interviewing for other jobs, and attendance at the company's San Francisco headquarters has fallen sharply, according to people familiar.

Frustration has boiled over into distrust of Pathak's leadership for some employees, while others hope Pathak can secure funding to repay workers and bring the company back to financial health. In conversations and memos, Pathak says that he is highly invested in securing Foundation's future, the people said.

Despite the firm's shaky finances, Foundation continued to hire for open roles until recently and some new workers have never been fully paid, said the people.

To keep employees from leaving before a possible Base Group investment, Pathak has floated the idea of offering workers equity in the startup, the people said.

At the same time, human resources staff have warned workers against taking legal action with California to recover their wages, saying that any employees who file complaints with the state would be dismissed, the people said.

Following a Nov. 14 CNBC report detailing the missed payrolls and a $4.6 million loan Pathak took from the startup in 2025, the chief executive addressed the issue in an all-hands meeting, according to the people.

Pathak defended the arrangement by telling workers that he had plowed his own money into the startup and takes only a nominal salary, the people said.

The co-founder also told employees who were in dire financial straits to contact human resources for help covering personal bills, the people added.

"I'm burning through savings just to afford my apartment," one employee told CNBC. "It's extremely unfortunate we're in this situation."

#365. Some U.S. food banks see demand top pandemic levels

During the Covid-19 pandemic, Greg Silverman watched an MTA bus driver pull over on Manhattan's Upper West Side, let his passengers off and run across the street toward him.

Silverman, who runs New York nonprofit West Side Campaign Against Hunger, initially thought the driver wanted to use the bathroom at the church where the food distribution was taking place. Instead, the man asked, "Can I get some food?"

"He was a full-time employee," Silverman said. "You are an essential personnel, making the city survive and you need food."

Now, Silverman said, his organization has seen demand surpass even the levels it observed during that time of crisis when the U.S. economy ground to a halt — and many of the people now seeking food also have jobs. Silverman expects the nonprofit to distribute as much as 6 million pounds of food this year.

"The height of the pandemic was not the height of need, by any means," he said.

The pressure on the emergency food system extends beyond New York. Nationally, use of charitable food programs remains elevated as sustained inflation makes it harder for Americans to afford food, housing and healthcare. Higher prices come at the same time that the federal government has restricted food aid.

The Department of Agriculture's latest annual report found that 13.7% of U.S. households, roughly 18.3 million households, experienced food insecurity in 2024. That rate was significantly higher than in every year from 2016 through 2021.

The pandemic initially brought a surge in demand for charitable food programs, which was followed by government support. In the years that followed, pandemic-era policies such as expanded Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, benefits, the enhanced child tax credit and school meal programs phased out as inflation spiked.

"This is not because you can't go to work," said City Harvest President Carlos Rodriguez. "Primarily, your work and your wages are just not keeping up with the way costs have gone up in the last five years alone."

City Harvest, which works with food providers across the five boroughs of New York, told CNBC 1 in 5 New Yorkers is currently experiencing food insecurity, or limited access to enough food because of a lack of money or other resources. That is up from 1 in 6 a year earlier, and 1 in 8 before the pandemic.

Average monthly visits to food pantries and soup kitchens in New York are also 85% higher than before the pandemic, said Rodriguez.

In the Federal Reserve's October Beige Book, the central bank's New York regional branch described a sharp rise in first-time food pantry users. One nonprofit leader told the Federal Reserve Bank of New York that the strain was comparable to the pandemic, "but without the same philanthropic and government support."

Data from Plentiful, a technology platform that connects people with food pantries and tracks their usage, also points to growing demand and limited resources.

"For pantries using our reservation and pre-registration features, we see that the overwhelming majority of those are at or over capacity," said Catherine Compitello, CEO of Plentiful. "Demand is growing while supply is not."

First-time users of Plentiful in New York City rose roughly 56% from August to October, Compitello said. It was the second-largest fall surge since 2016; the only larger one came during last year's federal government shutdown, when delayed SNAP benefits drove more people to seek food assistance.

Compitello said that when families have trouble affording essentials, they often prioritize healthcare, transportation, childcare and utilities, leaving food as the expense they cut back on.

Demand for food banks is rising in other regions of the country, and nonprofits are facing their own operational challenges as they try to meet it.

A spokesperson for the Los Angeles Regional Food Bank told CNBC the organization's diesel bill more than doubled in September, to roughly $75,000, adding to the cost of delivering food and running refrigerated trucks.

Demand in the region is also spiking. Distribution in the Los Angeles area for January through September totaled 116 million pounds of food and grocery products — the equivalent of 93 million meals — and slightly higher than a near-record year in 2025, according to the Los Angeles Regional Food Bank.

Federal food aid changes have exacerbated the problems. Rodriguez of City Harvest described SNAP as a first line of defense against hunger, saying the program can provide as many as nine meals for every one meal the organization provides. But City Harvest has estimated at least 8.7% of SNAP recipients in New York City lost benefits over the past year, after congressional Republicans and President Donald Trump approved work certification requirements and changes to eligibility.

The pressure is also mounting in Los Angeles County, where roughly 260,000 CalFresh recipients are subject to expanded federal work requirements that took effect in June. CalFresh is California's version of SNAP.

That does not mean all 260,000 will lose benefits, since people who meet the work requirements or qualify for an exemption can remain eligible. But a Los Angeles Regional Food Bank spokesperson told CNBC the changes add another layer of uncertainty for households already struggling with food costs.

In Atlanta, the pressure extends beyond the city itself to the surrounding region. The Atlanta Community Food Bank serves about 270,000 households a month, or nearly 700,000 people, through partner pantries across North Georgia. President and CEO Kyle Waide said the number of people it serves has jumped more than 70% in five years.

"Much of that increase is among people whose incomes are too high to qualify for federal benefit programs," said Waide.

Under current SNAP guidelines in Georgia, most households must have gross monthly income at or below 130% of the federal poverty level to qualify. They must also meet a separate net income test. For fiscal 2027, which began Oct. 1, the gross income limit is $2,960 a month for a household of three, or about $35,520 annually, and $3,575 a month for a household of four, or $42,900 a year.

More than 60% of Atlanta Community Food Bank clients have household incomes above the cutoff for SNAP eligibility, Waide said, generally in the mid-to-upper $30,000 range depending on household size. The food bank does not collect everyone's income, he said, but the figure is based on survey estimates.

Given those dynamics, Waide said he does not expect the need to ease.

"We're preparing for the level of demand to stay where it is today, or even increase more," Waide said. "We don't see a big source of relief coming anytime soon."

The full-suspension Current ADV is powered by a 750-watt motor between the cranks that delivers smooth pedal assistance over hill and dale, plus a boost mode for rocketing up the steep stuff. The battery is good for hours of riding; it can go over 100 miles on a charge in Eco mode, so your loved one can go even farther.

What’s a surefire gift for the person who is otherwise impossible to shop for? A good pair of sunglasses. The Minnesota company Article One has all of its glasses made in Japan to exacting standards. We especially like the Accord frames, with clean lines that give the specs an understated style that’s fashionable in nearly every situation. The lenses are made of TR-18 Tritan, a co-polyester material making waves in the eyewear industry that offers great visual clarity while being more durable than common tinted polycarbonate lenses.

Mostly known for his shiny and expensive pendants and lighting fixtures, Tom Dixon also designs fun—and affordable—items for around the house like this foot-tall cast-iron hand. Its powder-coated finish offers a little grip, making it the perfect perch for a phone, a notebook, or a wristwatch. A perfect gift for the person in your life with the funky taste who is otherwise impossible to shop for.

Handmade from slip-cast terra cotta in Eugene, Oregon, this donut-shaped lamp puts out 600 lumens of soft, warm light. A 6-watt LED sits inside the frosted globe, and you can dim it via a rotary switch on the power cord. It’s a functional and tiny (5.5 x 4.5-inch) beacon to beautify your loved one’s love nest.

The mobile technology company Nothing has been focusing on its audio prowess lately, and its new Headphone (1) Pro are evidence, catering to audio professionals in the studio chasing the best sound quality. With a triple-driver architecture in each ear and studio-quality tuning, these cans are a surprise hit with what WIRED reviewer Harry Rabinowitz called “outstanding” sound quality.

Once a niche category, Art TVs are now all the rage. These displays work like regular old boob tubes, but when you turn them off, their bezel-framed matte screens double as digital picture frames for fine art you can download. Samsung was early to the Art TV market, and its latest Frame Pro is its most gorgeous plug-and-play gallery yet. Art lovers will appreciate the bevy of options to show on the TV, with top-name painters and photographers available in Samsung’s store, as well as collections from The Met and MoMA. Sizes range from 55 to 85 inches, and wireless connections make setup a breeze.

Your photo-taking friend already has a few cameras. They have the big one with the fancy lenses, and the smaller one with the even fancier lenses. They shoot tons of pictures with their phone, too, of course. But the camera they really want is the Ricoh GR IV. Fans of this pocketable, high-end digital point-and-shoot are like a cult, the type of people who find each other at parties and whisper in the corner about this camera and how much it’s totally changed their game. We could list the specs and tell you what it can do, but you can read our review for all of that. The most important thing to know is that if you want to splurge on something nice for your friend who’s obsessively taking photos all the time, this is the perfect camera for them. Be their hero. (Note: Our review is of the previous model. This newer version has a highlight-diffusion filter that improves the camera’s performance in extreme light and dark conditions, making it even more desirable.)

There’s no shortage of beautiful, functional bags in our midst, but this zipper tote is one of our favorites. Nomadix makes blankets, towels, and bags from recycled materials, and the DayTripper's nylon shell and polyester interior are made from 100 percent recycled fabric. The ripstop face adds toughness as well as some visual flair. Inside are a padded laptop sleeve, two bottle sleeves, and a zipper pocket. The 26-liter capacity lets it do double duty as a commuter and a weekender.

For the trail runner in your life who gets up at dawn to put in serious miles in the wilderness, only the best shoes will do. These kicks from Norda are tough, light, and responsive. The uppers and laces are made from ecofriendly Dyneema, a highly durable all-weather fabric made from by-products of the wood and pulp industries. The soles are made by Vibram, a pioneer in those thin-but-springy soles that let the runner really feel the earth beneath their feet.

For a long time, wetsuits were made with neoprene, a petroleum-based product with an eco footprint that didn’t really square with surfing’s ocean-loving, conservation-minded vibe. Patagonia was early to the market with neoprene-free suits, and now the company has completely overhauled its wetsuit designs. The new Regulator collection—made from natural rubber and recycled nylon—has thicker insulation and padding where it’s needed most. The rest of the suit stays flexible and comfy to wear for long stretches. A big U-shaped zipper runs around the shoulders, making it easier for surfers to get it on and off in the parking lot. Comes in various thicknesses, and in men’s and women’s cuts.

Kindles have always been plasticky pieces of tech. However, now that Amazon’s hardware is under the eye of ex-Microsoft Surface hardware guru Panos Panay, the brand has been zhuzhing its devices. The basic Kindle now comes in an all-aluminum design. (You can still buy the plastic version for a little less cash.) It still lacks the warm light and auto-adjusting light of premium models, but you get double the storage, plus no ads. It's heavy in a good way, like a book, and the size is still just right for reading. It's a great upgrade for the book lover in your life—unless they've already converted to a non-Amazon e-reader.

Musicians and audio nerds alike flip out over Teenage Engineering’s fun and inventive approach to creative noisemaking. This little multipurpose box is the latest must-have for TE fans. It’s technically a speaker—powered by a 12-hour battery, with connections for whatever you can think to pair or plug in—but it doubles as an amplifier for musical performance. Plug in a guitar, bass, keyboard, or microphone and enjoy 35 watts of volume from the dual speakers (a 4-inch woofer and a 1-inch tweeter). Dial up onboard effects like distortion, echo, and reverb. When rock time is over, your musical loved one can attach the optional antenna ($29) and use it as an FM radio, or plug in the optional mic ($29) for some karaoke.

If you're always stealing your loved one's battery pack and leaving them with little charge left for their own devices, buy Nimble's SharePower for them (or yourself). This power bank splits into two, so you can always share power (get it) with someone else. Each half is 5,000 mAh, enough to recharge a smartphone. They combine magnetically for 10,000 mAh that can recharge your gadget twice. Nimble is also known for its sustainability chops, manufacturing the battery with 100 percent recycled plastic and shipping it in plastic-free packaging.

Aren't magnets amazing? Wandrd's new Magnetic Camera Straps prove that yet again. These straps have a magnetic attachment system that makes removing the camera a breeze. The magnets guide the strap into the anchor point, while a locking mechanism ensures the camera can’t fall off. If your loved one already has a camera strap they love, like a fancy leather strap, Wandrd sells cheap DIY kits so they can add the ingenious magnetic system to their own strap.

This 15-inch clock, dreamed up by Polish designer Marta Krupińska for Ikea’s latest PS collection, is designed to resemble a marine periscope. Whether placing this curvy clock on the bedside table will result in nautical dreams, we can’t say. However, we can tell you that it won’t disturb your loved one’s sleep; the quartz movement is entirely silent, with no ticktock sounds. Buy it in their favorite color, as long as it’s red.

The San Francisco producer Veso makes zippy aperitifs as well as vermouths with unconventional flavorings like fig leaf, miso, olive, and anchovy. This bottling, a limited 2026 release, is vermouth flavored with tomatoes. Early Girls and Purple Cherokees take a seven-month bath in grape spirits, then the liquid is pressed and mixed into a pinot blanc with kombu, beets, and carrots. The result is a pinkish vermouth with a salty, vegetal, and umami character that’s wholly unique. Get this for the adventurous drinker in your life, and settle in to enjoy some tomato gibsons, tomato-mezcal negronis, and tomato-wine spritzers.

The season’s hottest toy is a programmable, robotic duck. That’s not a joke: The Microduck is a funky little automaton made by the robotics team at the AI company Hugging Face. The 10-inch-tall bipedal bot has a camera and a lidar system to interact with its surroundings, plus two inertia sensors that help it right itself when it inevitably tips over. The little guy can even pick things up with its beak. Owners train their physical ducks using a virtual duck simulator on their computers. Since the Microducks are on backorder—new purchases will ship in the new year—your loved one can prepare for their robot’s arrival by using AI models to train up the duck and imagining all the things it can do.

This plug-and-play turntable makes a great starter record player for the vinyl-curious audiophile or a solid upgrade for the obsessive record collector. A built-in preamp lets the Spira connect directly to an existing stereo without additional equipment. It comes outfitted with a very nice Audio-Technica cartridge so they can spin their most precious platters on day one. It even has Bluetooth to connect to a speaker or wireless headphones. Aside from those conveniences, the Spira comes from Cambridge Audio, a British hi-fi brand known for high-quality, sweet-sounding components that keep performing for decades.

The horological aficionado on your list probably has a G-Shock—the iconic resin Casio was countless collectors’ first watch—but we’d doubt they have one of these. The new release ditches the digital readout for analog hands, handsomely encased in a shock-resistant, waterproof 44.5-millimeter case. A couple of complications round out the face: a sleepable second-hand dial and a date wheel in the eye at 3 o’clock. It comes in a variety of colors and materials, but this statement-worthy bright yellow version is our favorite.

Some folks are born with an eye for design, and some need solid training—preferably during the first couple years of life. Michelle Rial’s book presents familiar picture-book-for-kids fare (numbers, vocabulary, colors, feelings) as charts, diagrams, graphs, and infographics. While it does actually serve as a fine developmental learning tool for tots, we all know who the real audience for this book is. Get it for the person in your life at the center of the Venn diagram between “creative professional” and “new parent.”

TIRED: Retro arcade games. WIRED: Retro arcade games made of Lego bricks that you assemble yourself. Yes, this 15.5-inch play set actually works, giving you a wholly analog representation of the 1981 classic, Donkey Kong. It’s made up of 1,367 pieces, and includes working controls, three characters, and a mechanism to keep launching barrels into the scaffolding on a loop. Move the joystick and make Mario (aka Jumpman) leap over the barrels, climb to the top, and save the kidnapped Pauline.

If your loved one can’t start their day without a cup of pour-over coffee, this is the only brewing machine they’ll want. It automates the method of slowly pouring hot water over freshly ground beans. It even replicating the spiral pour pattern (hence the name) essential to pour-over brewing, as a swirl of the spout helps evenly distribute water to the grounds in the filter. The machine includes a bean grinder and a water tank, so one button push is all that’s needed for a cup or two of brightly flavored coffee.

The stepped shape of this stainless steel jigger is based on an antique measuring tool from the 1930s. The simple yet effective design makes eyeballing precise measurements exceptionally easy—especially helpful if the jigger has already gotten some use earlier in the evening. The steps are in half-ounce (15 milliliters) increments, with four indicators going up to a full 2 ounces (60 ml). Get one for the mixologist in your midst.

Here’s a fun idea for a connected device: The IDX is an analog gauge to display real-time data streams pulled from the internet. You can configure it out of the box to show the current temperature or air quality, the price of Bitcoin or $ANT, your home’s electricity use, or live download speeds. It can also be used as a focus timer. The digital face changes based on what data you’re displaying, but the big needle is completely mechanical, giving the data nerd in your home a way to monitor anything important to them without constantly pulling out their phone.

The world is awash in tools to generate music with AI, and the results are often lacking. Far more interesting is this tool your musical loved one can use to generate music with PI—plant intelligence. PlantWave is a small box with a pair of electrical sensors that attach to the leaves of any plant or mushroom. The box measures the subtle electrical signals the plant gives off and converts that into musical data. Assign that data stream to one of many digital instruments in the companion app, and listen to the plants sing. We originally tested the PlantWave several years ago, but the app has since blossomed to include more sounds and even lets creators craft their own digital instruments.

#359. AI Solved Math’s Most Famous Problem. Now Humans Are Struggling to Understand It

Mathematicians are struggling to decode a 17-million-line solution to their field’s most famous problem, published by an Anthropic researcher on Friday.

Levent Alpöge released a proof in the programming language Lean of the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis, which he had created with Claude. While the conjecture, which describes how prime numbers are distributed, is widely assumed to be true, many mathematicians have tried and failed to definitively show this, and the problem has become something of a holy grail of number theory.

Since Alpöge published his proof, more than 200 people have been collaborating to verify it. On Saturday, the nonprofit the Lean Focused Research Organization and volunteer-led organization Mathlib said on Saturday they have “full confidence” that the proof is sound. The problem is formulated correctly and the code compiles, they confirmed. Now, “we look forward to all the activity in the mathematical community that will help explain the new ideas in this proof,” they wrote.

Lean proofs are written to be checked by machine, while mathematical papers are written to explain the results to the community so that they can be reviewed and advanced. But Alpöge hasn’t released the paper version, which clocks in at 250,000 pages and is, in his own estimation, a “travesty of slop.” (On Monday, he added in an X post that the Lean proof “is full of garbage obviously” but that it still “compiles.” He also said that the 250,000 pages was a “joke … I find big number [sic] extremely hilarious.”) That’s left mathematicians to their own devices as they try to decipher what new findings they can obtain and build from the result.

“Knowing there is a proof is one thing,” Abhishek Saha, a professor of mathematics at Queen Mary University of London, tells WIRED, “but when we understand the proof, that would allow us to actually go beyond what has happened, to build new branches of mathematics perhaps or formulate the next conjecture to push the horizon further.”

Saha reckons the community effort should be able to simplify the result into a human-readable form of under 10,000, if not 1,000, pages. But complicating this feat is the fact that the proof appears to draw on many advanced branches of number theory in a long and “incredibly counterintuitive” argument. “I don't think this kind of proof would ever come from a human,” says Saha, “but AIs can do something completely different and almost alien, and that breaks our intuition about how very difficult mathematical results might come about.”

He was shocked to see even his own corner of number theory utilized by the proof, and has since been trying to understand how. Saha has been using OpenAI’s Astra model to convert sections of the Lean proof into more digestible formats, such as single-page posters like those presented at conferences and shorter documents. But there’s a limit to that approach.

“It may well be that no single person has the expertise to understand in detail every part of the proof,” he says.

More than 60 other individuals are using AI agents to try to translate the Lean lines into understandable ideas on Principia Math, a collaborative platform designed to facilitate the understanding of AI breakthroughs. So far, they have done this for more than 3,000 pieces of the Lean proof, though platform chief executive officer Anton Shakov expects it will take mathematicians months before they have a good conceptual understanding of the proof Alpöge produced with Claude in roughly six weeks. “I personally believe the picture we will get in the end, once the ideas of this proof have been properly understood, will be astoundingly beautiful," he tells WIRED.

Independent mathematicians have already understood and written up one smaller result to have come out of Alpöge’s proof.

AI labs have previously been criticized for rushing to publish breakthrough mathematical results, claiming glory while leaving the academic community to digest the results—and clean up mistakes.

“No human being can reasonably claim to be responsible for, or even to understand, such a document,” the Association for Human Mathematics, a group of more than 1,000 mathematicians founded in September, wrote in a statement on Friday of the 17-million-line opus. It complained that Alpöge’s announcement “builds upon over a century of human work, but fails to advance mathematical understanding in the same way.”

Alpöge, who before joining Anthropic was a researcher at Harvard University, acknowledged on Friday what an “extraordinary” situation it was to present “the world with a complete argument before having mastered a massive neighborhood around its mathematics,” and wrote that he would try his best to help digest the proof, including by writing it up properly. But having had to hold off from making the announcement ahead of Anthropic’s initial public offering on Thursday, “I just could not live if I waited even longer,” he wrote.

Anthropic rival OpenAI in October proved a weaker version of the problem, called the quasi-Riemann hypothesis. Alpöge had been scooped by OpenAI in September on another Millennium Prize Problem concerning the Navier-Stokes equations, which describe fluid motion. When the company said it had solved part of the problem, Alpöge’s collaborator, New York University professor Tristan Buckmaster, claimed OpenAI had rushed ahead to beat the pair to it after becoming aware of his work. The pair also announced on Friday that they had completed the remaining unsolved parts of the Navier-Stokes problem.

#357. Best Buy reports comparable sales growth of 6.1%, highest in five years

Best Buy on Tuesday beat Wall Street expectations on the top and bottom lines for its third fiscal quarter and raised its full-year guidance.

The consumer electronics retailer reported comparable sales growth of 6.1%, a significant beat over expectations of 2.3%, according to market intelligence platform StreetAccount. The company said that growth was its highest in five years. It reported a domestic comparable sales increase of 6.2% and international comparable sales growth of 4.9%.

"We have a tremendous amount of momentum," CEO Jason Bonfig told CNBC. "The fact that we saw pretty much broad-based growth across almost all of our categories is a lot of momentum that we're very excited about."

Best Buy also raised its guidance for the rest of the year. It's now expecting full-year revenue of between $43 billion and $43.3 billion compared with a previous expectation of between $42.3 billion and $42.8 billion. It's expecting comparable sales to be up 3.4% to 4% compared with prior guidance of between 1.9% and 3%.

The earnings report is the company's first since Bonfig took over as CEO from Corie Barry at the beginning of the month.

Bonfig said the retailer saw overperformance in both computing and gaming for the quarter, driven by recent game launches and a targeted product assortment.

Looking ahead into the holiday season, he said the Best Buy consumer remains "resilient," but that they are focused on getting value wherever they can.

"We did see not only our current customers continue to be engaged, but we actually did see more new customers come into the brand, as well as we had some customers that we re-engaged as well," Bonfig said. "So those are really, really positive signs for us in Q3, and all of that was factored into the way that we guided for Q4 and the rest of the year."

Here's how the company performed in the period ended Oct. 31 compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

Best Buy reported net income of $353 million, or $1.66 per share, compared with $140 million, or 66 cents per share, the year prior. Adjusting for one-time items, including restructuring charges, Best Buy posted adjusted earnings of $1.62 per share.

Revenue rose to $10.24 billion from $9.67 billion in the year-ago period. Best Buy reported domestic revenue of $9.42 billion and international revenue of $820 million.

Tuesday's earnings are the latest in a series of strong reports from the retailer, which has been instituting a turnaround strategy to return to growth after getting hit by declining foot traffic, lower consumer sentiment, tariffs and memory costs.

Shares of Best Buy are up nearly 45% this year.

Bonfig told CNBC last quarter that the launch of "Grand Theft Auto VI" in the current quarter is expected to drive sales in the gaming category, which has been seeing gains over the past year. Last month, Best Buy launched a new gaming experience for customers featuring gaming content, technology and special offers, among other features.

"I think there'll still be opportunities for gaming to continue to drive our business moving forward," Bonfig told CNBC on Tuesday.

#356. Election Deniers Despair Because Even Donald Trump Isn’t Buying What They’re Selling

With his head in his hands, Joe Oltmann cut a dejected figure. For weeks, the seasoned election denier had promoted the baseless conspiracy theory that the midterms were rigged. He said he had sent the White House a 75-page report laying out in excruciating detail a conspiracy theory about how former Venezuelan officials had infiltrated the US electoral system to rig the outcome in favor of the Democrats. (There is no evidence to support this theory.) He had even, he claimed, spoken on the phone to President Donald Trump.

But two weeks after the election, nothing had been done.

In the wake of the overwhelming victory for the Democrats in the midterm elections, Trump has broadly appeared to accept the results, claiming the losses were the result of his name not appearing on the ballot. While he shared some election conspiracy theories in the days after the election, he’s taken very little action since.

Oltmann is among a group of influential election deniers who believe, without evidence, that the midterms were rigged and who claim to be in direct contact with Trump, but are frustrated by the president’s lack of fervor or seeming interest in overturning the results. These figures are making increasingly desperate demands of the president, including declaring martial law and ordering military tribunals.

“We can walk into every voting [location] and say: ‘Take this equipment, throw it out in the street,’” says Oltmann. “We can do that … that's not violent … We're just doing our jobs as Americans.”

These calls for action echo very similar demands made in the weeks leading up to the January 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, and some of the same figures are involved—though allies in the administration that once boosted their lies appear to have gone silent.

“This is a carbon copy of 2020,” said Patrick Byrne, the founder of Overstock.com who claims to have spent $100 million on promoting election integrity over the last six years, on a podcast on Saturday. He also claimed that, two weeks before the attack on the Capitol, he was in a room with Trump advocating for the same measures he is asking Trump to take now.

The big difference this time around, however, is that, so far, Trump has not been leading the charge. In the weeks after his election loss to former president Joe Biden in 2020, Trump was quick to seize on claims that the election had been rigged. In the lead-up to this year’s midterms, Trump and his administration did everything they could to promote baseless conspiracy theories about noncitizens and mail-in voting; they also weaponized the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Justice to target those they believed were responsible.

Days after the election this month, as the midterm results rolled in, Trump shared screenshots of X posts from election deniers on his Truth Social account, boosting baseless conspiracy theories about the midterms.

On November 9, he appeared to be ready to embrace those conspiracy theories, writing on Truth Social: “Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong??? Some early voting “dumps” were so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote. It’s all about the machines, which are far more important than the voter! President DJT.”

Election deniers on X and Telegram celebrated, believing that Trump was about to fully endorse their community once again. But in the weeks since, Trump has refrained from posting much of anything about stolen or rigged elections, save for a few limited references.

“I am going to give evidence to the president today … I have a wealth of evidence,” Peter Ticktin, a lawyer and former schoolfriend of Trump, told WIRED in an interview on November 11. Ticktin refused to share the evidence with WIRED and said the documents came from “various sources, some who prefer to be anonymous.”

Ticktin also said he would speak directly to Trump about the issues and would be advocating for the president to “nullify all of the results of the last election and declare martial law.” Ticktin told WIRED on Monday that he had not yet spoken with the president and was hoping to soon. Ticktin appears resigned: “If we take him for what he's saying at this point in time, he's not planning to do anything beyond cooperate with the globalists.”

While many on the right have followed Trump’s lead in ignoring claims about rigged midterms, a significant number of Republicans believe that the midterm votes were not “free and fair,” according to a new poll from UC San Diego.

Major election deniers are split over what to do now. Byrne, for example, disagrees with Oltmann’s suggestion to seize voting machines—but he has another plan: reinstate Michael Flynn, a prolific election denier, to his former role as Trump’s national security adviser.

“Instead of going straight to insurrection, [Trump] uses current authorities to go inspect hard drives in 12 cities, and you bring Michael Flynn in as national security adviser, and then turn it over to Michael. Michael can get this all done by December 1,” Byrne said over the weekend. “If you do find foreign activity … then say, OK, I'm nullifying this election, I'm declaring a new election in 120 days.”

But there is no indication from the administration that anything like this will happen, and Flynn himself has called the election “a master class by the GOP in how to fail.” The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

#355. IHOP is launching its first-ever collectible holiday mug — how to shop the ultra-limited drop

IHOP is officially entering the holiday merch wars, but keeping supplies super thin.

Starting Nov. 30, IHOP is launching its inaugural Collector’s Holiday Mug for $15 at participating restaurants nationwide. The catch? Each IHOP location is receiving just 24 mugs for the entire holiday season, making this the first-ever branded merchandise item sold inside IHOP dining rooms.

At just $15, it undercuts virtually every rival coffeehouse collector mug on the market, including the new Starbucks FriendsWithYou ceramic mug. And you're not forced to buy a pricey combo meal or download a loyalty app just to unlock access.

The real issue is that 24 mugs per restaurant is virtually nothing.

Once the first 24 mugs at your local IHOP sell out on Nov. 30, they are gone for good. There are no online restocks, no mobile-order reservations, and no second shipments scheduled for December. If you genuinely want one for your shelf or a holiday gift, you will need to visit a participating restaurant in person right when doors open on Nov. 30. The only alternative is to pay obnoxious reseller markups, and nobody wants that.

Joseph Green is the Global Shopping Editor for Mashable. He covers VPNs, headphones, fitness gear, dating sites, streaming, and shopping events like Black Friday and Prime Day.

#354. A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks

Technology called “machine perfusion” is creating the chance for more transplants—and daring new science.

Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive, on life support, outside the body for seven weeks, opening up speculative new possibilities in biomedical engineering.

The feat, whose details are pending publication, was carried out in Sydney after a team led by surgeon and inventor Carlo Pulitano connected a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste.

In an interview, Pulitano, a transplant surgeon at the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital and a professor at the University of Sydney, likened the life support system to “an artificial body.” Its official name is the Extended Organ Perfusion System.

“Our group is the only one in the world to have maintained a human liver under fully normothermic, physiological conditions for seven weeks,” he says.

Normothermic means body temperature, or about 37 °C. The previous record for keeping an internal organ alive outside the body was set in Switzerland several years ago. That organ—also a liver—lasted around two weeks.

Most organs destined for transplant survive only a few hours in special ice buckets and need to be raced to their destination. Over the last decade, however, surgeons have been switching to perfusion systems, which pump warm or cold fluids into an organ. This can double the time it can be held before it must be transplanted.

Pulitano says the key to breaking the record was to automate the systems used to keep the organ thriving. During a meeting in Switzerland earlier this year, the Sydney team described perfusing 55 human livers, one after the other. Some were connected to a system that needed to be adjusted manually, but for those placed on the automated system—which produced the seven-week survivor—the average survival time tripled, to about four weeks.

Perfusion has already enabled doctors to restart hearts from dead people and keep them beating outside the body. Paulo Martins, a transplant doctor at the University of Oklahoma, says about half the kidneys he transplants are now perfused, even though the process can add $100,000 to the cost of a transplant.

While the research awaits formal publication, the eventual goal is what Pulitano and colleagues call “time-unlimited liver preservation.”

Scientists have already discovered possible medical benefits to keeping organs on life support longer than usual. One, they say, is that perfused organs apparently start to repair themselves and become stronger after a day or so. That’s what led a Swiss team, in 2022, to transplant a damaged liver that had been kept on perfusion for three days—the longest time any internal organ had remained outside the body before a successful transplant, says Waldemar Hoffmann, the CEO and cofounder of Apersys, a startup formed to commercialize the technology.

Pulitano says his own startup, Aeternum Life Technologies, will be helping with a planned trial in Sydney to transplant low-quality livers kept on perfusion for four days.

What’s less clear, says Hoffmann, is whether any transplant surgeon would ever want, or need, to use an organ kept alive for nearly two months. He says people in the field believe Pulitano’s record is real, but they don’t know how healthy the organ was at the end or even what so much extra time is likely to achieve. “The key question is what the purpose for a seven-week perfusion would be,” he says.

Yet that’s where things could start to get interesting, says Martins, the Oklahoma surgeon. Long-term life support could enable far-out concepts like artificial wombs, new types of organ manufacturing, and the chance to experiment directly on human organs outside the body for extended periods.

For his part, Pulitano says long-term machine perfusion could help grow new organs. In living donations, surgeons commonly take half of a person’s liver to give someone else. After about two months, both parts will have grown back almost to their full volume. Pulitano says he’s tried dividing a liver and then attaching the sections to the machine. If that works, he says, it could be a way to multiply one donor liver into several full-size organs.

“It’s important to have people thinking outside the box and pushing the limits and creating possibilities for things that, right now, sometimes we don’t even have a need for but are going to be needed in the future,” says Martins. “That’s how science moves.”

He’s not the only one who thinks so. For instance, a US company, Bexorg, has been reanimating human brains using perfusion pumps. The idea is to study what effects experimental drugs have on them. That company perfuses brains for about a day but has said it wants to extend the time to two weeks.

Similar experiments can be done on livers, says Pulitano, who has already tried adding gene therapies to the organs. “It gives us a living human organ model for translational research that no animal system can match, because the biology, the immunology, and the drug responses are human from the outset,” he says.

Meanwhile, in Silicon Valley, patents filed by Altos Labs, a billionaire-backed longevity startup, describe attempts to introduce reprogramming genes into animal livers maintained outside the body. Eventually, Altos scientists have speculated, they might temporarily disconnect a failing organ while it’s still in a person’s body, connecting it to a perfusion machine in order to douse it with ultra-powerful genetic treatments without risking the rest of the body.

Doctors probing the limits of organ life support have now formed two new scientific societies to explore the concept. One, founded by Martins and called the International Society for Organ Preservation and Perfusion Therapy, will hold its inaugural meeting this year in Italy. The other, based in China, was launched in August to advance what doctors at the First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-Sen University have termed “organ medicine”: research at the level of whole organs kept alive by “bionic maintenance.”

“What is exploding is the idea of this technology that clearly goes beyond simply organ preservation,” says Pulitano. “Basically, that’s a concept that’s entirely new.”

Scientists hope it could be used to reconstruct a person’s inner thoughts, mental images, or even dreams.

#353. COP31 climate talks end without consensus on how to fund vulnerable countries or move the world away from coal, oil and gas use

After two weeks of tough talks, the COP31 climate summit has closed without a consensus on how to quit fossil fuels or fund countries struggling to adapt to a hotter world.

Almost two days into overtime, climate talks in the Turkish city of Antalya have collapsed as countries led by the European Union rejected a deal that critics say undermines the shift away from planet-heating fossil fuels.

After two weeks of tough negotiations, the EU said it could not support the proposed agreement, known as the Antalya Pact, put forward by the COP presidency, saying it does not respond to the science.

"We will not endorse a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels, the driver of climate change. And we will not accept negotiating backward in time," said Irish climate minister Darragh O'Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU on Sunday.

He said adopting a decision that omitted fossil fuels would be "unconscionable" and risked "deepening the chasm between global commitment and the action required."

Panama also rejected the deal, describing it as a step backwards in addressing the climate crisis, and adding that any decision must acknowledge "the truth about the collective failure on 1.5 degrees Celsius [2.7 degrees Fahrenheit]." That is the threshold outlined in the 2015 Paris Agreement to avert runaway climate change.

"Those who contributed to this crisis ... must shoulder the responsibility to deal with it," the Panamanian delegation said.

The Marshall Islands, which faces an existential threat from sea level rise, formally objected to the cover decision, saying "we will not compromise our future to benefit fossil fuel interests."   Chris ⁠Bowen, Australia's COP31 negotiating president ‌⁠said the breakdown in talks was very ‌disappointing. Russia, however, supported the decision to leave out wording on accelerating a phaseout of fossil fuels, arguing that they are still a necessary power source and that each country should be able to determine its own pathway on how to cut emissions.

Pakistan and Ghana, defended the agreement as a necessary compromise in the spirit of multilateralism. "We need to build bridges not barriers," said the Pakistan negotiator.

The marathon talks, held at a time when the window is rapidly closing to avoid the escalating impacts of climate change, including drought, deadly heat and flooding, also saw major disputes over financing.   Developing states blamed the collapse in talks on the EU and other wealthier nations for failing to scale up financing to help them adapt to climate-linked weather extremes and the damage they cause. The EU is the largest provider of climate finance and has resisted new adaptation finance targets.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Harjeet Singh of the Fill the Fund campaign accused wealthy countries of demanding greater climate ambition while refusing to stump up the cash to pay for it.

"You can't ask developing countries to transform their economies while they're drowning in disasters and debt," he added.

The final cover decision had proposed further discussions on "an implementation pathway for tripling adaptation finance by 2035" but without mentioning a figure. It noted that developing countries need some $300 billion annually for adaptation until 2035, and expressed concern about "the gap between climate finance flows and needs."

Outside formal negotiations, a separate initiative to Transition Away from Fossil Fuels (TAFF) has been gaining momentum.

Maina Talia, Tuvalu's minister for climate change and the environment, said TAFF was "moving beyond debating whether fossil fuels are simply mentioned in a text, to creating detailed plans for a global transformation."

At the same time, a growing number of states, including Ireland, Denmark, the Netherlands, France, Germany and Finland, have either completed or are working on so-called national roadmaps to wean themselves off fossil fuels. But Brandon Wu, director of Policy and Campaigns ActionAid USA, dismissed such plans as "meaningless" and "nothing more than restatements of inadequate existing policy" on the part of rich countries not stepping up on climate finance. "COP31 was one of the worst COPs ever, and it's because the EU and other developed countries came with zero spirit of solidarity, cooperation or compromise. They may as well have come to the COP shouting at vulnerable communities: 'we don't care if you die.'"

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The rejected cover decision had recognized that electrification can deliver emissions reductions, improve energy security and expand access to energy.

It included a call to increase the share of electricity in final energy demand from around 20% now to 35% by 2035 — a proposal heavily touted by co-host Turkey. Still, about 75 countries, including solar powerhouse China, adopted the pledge outside of the formal negotiations. It is non-binding and does not specify whether that additional electricity must come from clean sources. Critics say this leaves open the possibility that expanded electricity demand could be met by fossil fuels.

The talks in Turkey marked the first time a COP was taking place under the explicit knowledge that global temperatures will exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. Countries were split on how to deal with that so-called "overshoot."

The cover decision had called on states to commit to limiting overshoot , acknowledging that every increment of warming above current levels would "result in increasingly adverse, and in some cases irreversible, impacts and risks to human and natural systems.”

It also recognized the need for "deep, rapid ​and ‌sustained" emissions cuts and for action on ramping down potent greenhouse gas methane.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Another contenious issue at the talks and in the final draft decision was a call for "increasing" carbon capture and storage technologies that entails capturing CO2 and burying it. The text said the world should aim to reach "gigaton scale" by 2035.

Scientists say some carbon removal technologies will be necessary to curb emissions and bring temperatures back down. But critics argue they are unproven at scale, expensive and risk giving polluters an excuse to keep burning fossil fuels.

Vanuatu's climate minister Ralph Regenvanu said carbon capture and storage "had been singled out for special attention that it doesn't deserve."

The stakes were high at COP31. The summit followed a string of recent climate-related disasters, from deadly heat waves in Europe to a glacier collapse in Nepal that killed more than 1,400 people.

At the same time, geopolitical shocks that sent oil prices rising globally shifted the focus onto energy security and the future of fossil fuels.

Speaking near the end of the conference in Antalya, Ethiopian foreign minister Gedion Timothewos, who will preside over COP32, said his country aimed to "restore hope, rebuild trust and mobilize collective action" at the next summit to be held in 2027 in the Ethiopian capital Addis Ababa.

"We will work with you all to rebuild confidence in multilateral climate cooperation. This confidence must be earned through delivery. The decisions we take at COPs must advance climate action and implementation."

With reporting from Tim Schauenberg and Katharina Schantz in Antalya.

#351. Don’t Bring Up AI if You Want to Enjoy Your Thanksgiving

Sophie has never used ChatGPT or Claude. “When I'm Googling, I type in ‘minus AI’ after every single search I do,” says the 27-year-old social work student, who lives in North Carolina. “I have deactivated Microsoft Copilot, all the things.”

The reasons behind her firm opposition to AI are multifold. She worries about the degradation of critical thinking and cognitive functioning, some AI leaders’ alignment with the Trump administration, and the environmental impact of data centers, particularly on the water supply in nonwhite communities. Her perspective is born of strong ideological convictions: “My anti-AI stance is very deeply ingrained in my anti-capitalist beliefs,” she says.

Though her parents and siblings are more or less on the same page, the AI use among her extended family is “pervasive.” She worries her aunt might be “bordering on AI psychosis.” And one of her cousins, a new mother of twins, created her babies’ “entire feeding and sleeping schedule” using ChatGPT and has invested in an app that uses AI to run pediatric doctor assessments.

The stark difference in opinion between Sophie and her relatives can make for some pretty tense family gatherings—something she’s dreading going into Thanksgiving. The topic “comes up every time” they get together. “I’m constantly anticipating frustration and being judged, being told that I am naive,” she says.

AI has been the focus of many an argument in Sophie’s family in recent years. (She and other interviewees chose to use pseudonyms or only first names to prevent further such conflict.) At a family get-together a couple of years ago, Sophie sent her résumé to her family members to get feedback, and the same cousin who uses ChatGPT for her babies’ meal schedule immediately fed the document to ChatGPT. “She didn't ask for my consent to use my intellectual property to train large learning language models,” Sophie says, which started a “huge conflict.” That cousin’s tech founder husband, she adds, asks snarky questions meant to poke holes in her stance, such as “Well, what about if it's a poor Black person in Africa using AI to create wealth for themselves?” And though Sophie successfully convinced a different cousin to stop using ChatGPT, that cousin immediately switched over to Claude, which Sophie describes as “a total white-liberal move to pick the better-branded version of the same evil tool.”

Over the past decade, the US’ chaotic, increasingly polarized political climate has put American families to the test: Trump, immigration, Israel and Palestine, the war in Iran, abortion, and LGBTQ rights are just a few issues that have turned holidays into yelling matches and siblings into strangers. This Thanksgiving, you might want to add AI to the list of topics to avoid bringing up around the table.

“It's the latest generational beef,” says Matt Lundquist, a psychologist and the founder and clinical director of Tribeca Therapy in New York City. He has found that arguments over AI are on the rise—especially among families.

Lundquist says the issue has “created a rupture,” even among people who are normally on the same page. This is the case for Lindsay, a 40-year-old romance novelist in Pennsylvania whose family is “very politically aligned.” Before AI became a hot-button issue, Lindsay says, her family “never had a conversation where you have to be like, ‘Nobody bring up politics. Nobody bring up Israel. Nobody bring up Trump.’” So she was surprised to find herself at odds with her uncle during Passover dinner when he began raving about what he believes are the wonders of ChatGPT.

As a professional writer, she was upset by her uncle's celebration of AI. Last year, Lindsay found out a book she wrote was used to train AI models. “I was like, ‘Do you understand that ChatGPT is not a magical device? It is being created by pirating work from actual writers.” She tried to convey the message that by using AI, “You're directly harming me.”

Her uncle was “befuddled” by her reaction and became “giggly and nervous.” This seemed to be the first time he’d heard that AI is trained on the intellectual property of real people left uncredited and uncompensated. “When I'm telling him this, I can see it's really not landing,” she says. “I can tell that he thinks this is a benevolent, harmless thing.”

Others in creative fields report running into similar arguments with older relatives, particularly those earlier in their careers. For John, a 20-year-old cinematography student in Chicago whose girlfriend works in animation, AI brings up fears around both his own career and the future of art. He says his dad, a civil and chemical engineer who works in the chemical plant industry, holds AI to a high regard and uses it to offload some of the work of managing plants around the country, organizing data—which makes his job more manageable.

“It can get heated,” says John. “I'll say, ‘Oh, this is potentially taking away my job.’ And his response will be like, ‘Well, I don't think that it'll get to that point.’ But then I'll say, ‘Oh, it's already doing that.’” From there, the discussion deteriorates: “Our positions are so ingrained,” he says.

“Folks under 30 are giving their parents shit about some of this stuff,” says Lundquist, who has found that anti-AI sentiment is resonant among young adults, particularly those new to the job market and who haven’t bought a home or raised children. This tracks with research from Pew published in August, which found that a majority of American adults under 30 describe themselves as more concerned than excited about AI—and 73 percent of the same group believe AI will result in fewer jobs. (At the same time, young people are still using AI. Axios reported in August that 61 percent of 18- to 34-year-old respondents to its poll said they'd used ChatGPT in the past month, while 48 percent said they’d used Gemini, and 20 percent had used Claude.)

Luke, a 23-year-old living in Toronto, says AI has become “the most debated topic in the household by far.” Luke just completed a degree in sports media and is struggling to find an entry-level job. Meanwhile, his dad, who has had a full career in computer science and web development, sees AI “as the next big step for every single person in the world.”

Debates over AI are “infecting all of our conversations,” Luke says. Last year, Luke remembers, at Canadian Thanksgiving, “what started off as just a discussion about my career and where I'm going next turned into a discussion about AI.”

“He wants what's best for me,” Luke says. He assumes his dad worries that taking an anti-AI stance could be “detrimental to my career and making a livelihood.”

In the family of Kaleigh, a 26-year-old living in Vermont and working toward a master’s degree in social work, disagreement about AI also falls along this parent-child fault line. The anti-AI stance of her and her younger brother is dismissed by her parents as “a young-person-exclusive take.”

When Kaleigh last returned to her parents’ house, her mother told her that ChatGPT had helped her redesign their backyard. This upset Kaleigh, as a close friend of hers is working toward a degree in landscape architecture. “It's an art form,” Kaleigh says. “It feels so out of touch or annoying to me to have somebody that has actual money not want to pay somebody to do something creative just because it's easier to access with this data thing.”

Lundquist has found that many older adults are “clueless” about how real the threat of AI feels to younger relatives. “I think if you own your second or third home with a 2.8 percent interest rate and you've already sent your kids to college, you're not worried about this stuff,” he says. “And so the fact that an AI bot can order your groceries for you is just kind of cool.”

His advice? Maybe avoid the topic altogether. “If it’s done in the genuine spirit of connection, learning, and exchanging ideas, that’s great,” he says. “If it’s done in the spirit of ‘This is going to be the 2026 Thanksgiving throwdown,’ that’s probably not very fruitful.”

If you do decide to go at it, he suggests getting in touch with what you’re actually fighting about. “When people are fighting about things like this, in reality they're probably fighting about other things,” he says. “The real beef is, ‘I’m mad about the pittance you and your generation have left for me. I’m mad about how the world seems to be not rewarding the kinds of things I anticipated it would and the things you anticipated it would as my parents.’”

Intergenerational fights about AI “hang on a desire to be understood,” he says. “So Dad picking up Claude and asking it for a sweet potato recipe burns in ways that feel like, ‘What the fuck, are you not paying attention?’”
